items.stem: FORECAST.ETS is most appropriate when the historical series:

options.text: Has a repeating seasonal pattern over a consistent timeline
options.rationale: Correct: FORECAST.ETS models trend and seasonality on a consistent time series.

options.text: Has no time dimension at all

options.rationale: It forecasts numeric values over time.
A single value cannot be forecast with seasonality.

items.explanation: Correct: FORECAST.ETS is designed for time series with trend and seasonality on a consistent timeline.

items.stem: Which TWO are good practices when using Copilot to help build an Excel forecast? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Recompute or spot-check any formula Copilot proposes
options.rationale: Correct: Copilot output must be verified against a manual check.

options.text: State the assumptions and data range in the prompt
options.rationale: Correct: clear, grounded prompts give more reliable assistance.

options.text: Publish Copilot's number without any review
Assume Copilot has calibrated the forecast's accuracy
options.rationale: Copilot does not guarantee calibrated accuracy.

items.explanation: Correct: verify Copilot's formulas and give it a clear, grounded prompt; never publish unreviewed output.

items.stem: Why prefer a two-variable data table over changing inputs one at a time?

options.text: It shows the combined effect of two drivers across a grid of values
options.rationale: Correct: a two-variable table reveals interaction across a grid.

options.text: It is the only way Excel can multiply
options.rationale: Excel multiplies directly; this is about sensitivity analysis.

options.text: It removes the need for any assumptions
It guarantees the forecast is correct

items.explanation: Correct: a two-variable data table shows the combined effect of two drivers across a grid of values.
